TAMPA, Florida: A US judge in Florida on Thursday (Nov 19) declared Thomas Markle, the estranged father of Britain's Duchess of Sussex, Meghan Markle, to be mentally competent to answer to a federal court charge accusing him of being a child sexual predator. Accepting the findings of a court-appointed forensic psychiatrist, US Magistrate Judge Lindsay Griffin ruled the 82-year-old father-in-law of Prince Harry was mentally fit to understand the proceedings against him and to properly assist in his own defence, court records showed. Neither prosecutors nor the defence disputed the findings of the psychiatrist's evaluation, contained in a 15-page report and based in large part on the doctor's in-person interview with Markle in prison last week. Markle was charged on Nov 5 in a criminal complaint with a single felony count of possessing child sexual abuse images.

According to an FBI affidavit filed with the complaint, the material in question, including two explicit photos of Markle posed with a naked underage girl and other images of him with children in various stages of undress, was found in two Los Angeles storage units. Commenting on the case at the time of Markle's arrest on Nov 6 at an assisted-living centre in Florida, FBI Director Kash Patel said Markle had "targeted innocent children and sought to steal their innocence through his criminal actions". Griffin's ruling capped a competency proceeding set in motion by the judge after Markle's first court hearing on the day of his arrest. In ordering a psychiatric examination of the defendant, Griffin wrote that she found "reasonable cause" to believe Markle was suffering from some mental deficiency, based in part on his advanced age and "lack of recall" during his first court appearance the day of his arrest. Dr Aime Gerodimos, who conducted the evaluation, wrote in her report that Markle appeared to suffer from a "major neurocognitive disorder," possibly the result of mild vascular disease. She also found he was likely "exaggerating deficits" when asked to recall specifics of the allegations against him. The psychiatrist concluded that Markle "does have sufficient present ability to understand the nature and consequences of the proceedings against him and to assist properly in his defence" - the legal standard for a criminal defendant to be deemed competent.

Related:

Thomas Markle, father of Meghan, cut off his ankle monitor, DOJ says

Meghan Markle's father arrested in US over child sex abuse images

CASE ORIGINATED IN PHILIPPINES Markle was first taken into custody at the assisted-living facility where he was residing in Lakeland, Florida, near Tampa. Griffin initially ordered him placed under home confinement on the condition that Markle wear an electronic monitoring device. But days later, the judge revoked the arrangement and ordered him back to jail without bond after Markle cut off his electronic ankle tag with a knife . It remained unclear when Markle would be transferred to federal custody in California, where the case against him was lodged. The judge on Thursday set a preliminary hearing in the case for Dec 1 in Tampa. According to the FBI affidavit, federal agents acting on a search warrant earlier this month seized a large cache of slides, film negatives and books from two storage lockers Markle had rented in Los Angeles since 2008. One of the photos showed a naked girl in a room that appears to be part of a motel chain in the Philippines, where Markle previously resided and where authorities initiated an investigation of him last month, the affidavit said. Philippine police said on Wednesday criminal complaints had been filed against Markle in the country’s Cebu province, where he lived. The complaints accuse Markle of violating local laws against online sexual abuse and exploitation of children, police said. Markle has denied the allegations, telling the Daily Mail the claims were untrue and describing them as "sick lies." Meghan Markle, an American actor, has been estranged from her father since the run-up to her marriage to King Charles' younger son, Harry, in 2018, when the duchess has said she first became aware of the allegations against her father. She has said she was "deeply distressed" over the matter, which led her to cut off contact between her father and her two children, Archie, 7, and Lilibet, 5.

Source: Reuters/nh

Trump administration weighs forcing US firms to disclose Chinese AI use

WASHINGTON: The Trump administration is considering requiring US companies to publicly disclose their use of Chinese AI models, a bid to discourage reliance on the technology without imposing new restrictions that could anger industry or Beijing, three people told Reuters. The Treasury Department and the White House Office of Science and Technology Policy (OSTP) have discussed the plan, which would apply to companies such as Airbnb, the people said. The company uses Qwen, an AI model made by China's Alibaba, to power its AI customer service agent. Under the plan, companies like Airbnb would be required to post that information on their websites. It was not immediately clear if the idea was gaining traction within the administration or if it would be enshrined in a formal rulemaking process if it does move forward.

But its consideration, first reported by Reuters, underscores an emerging push within the administration toward combating the spread of powerful Chinese open weight models, a source of deep concern within the government. Open weight models make their core components publicly available for anyone to download and adapt. The proposal also shows officials are looking at ways to discourage use of Chinese AI through a "name and shame" campaign while sticking to a broader anti-regulation stance on AI. The White House, the Treasury Department and Alibaba did not respond to requests for comment. Airbnb said in a statement that its AI activity "runs overwhelmingly on US-origin models" and the company uses "only a limited number of China-origin models, all of which are open-source and run only through approved US-based service providers, keeping data and operations separate and protected". The Chinese Embassy in Washington said Beijing opposes politicising trade and tech issues, which will "only stifle global AI advances and serve no one's interests. We will resolutely safeguard Chinese businesses' lawful rights and interests", it added. The consideration comes as revelations about Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s affair with an alleged Chinese spy have fueled renewed calls in Washington for a tougher stance on China . They have turned a spotlight on cases of Nvidia AI chips being smuggled to China that went unpunished, dialing up pressure on the Trump administration to crack down on Chinese tech threats.

Also read:

China's access to Nvidia chips in doubt as curbs gain traction in US Congress

Nvidia faces deepening scrutiny over China chip ties, CEO affair

Chinese-made open-weight models are gaining ground with US companies because they are cheaper than proprietary AI tools from top US labs OpenAI and Anthropic, and perform well enough. But China hawks fear Beijing is using such models - like Moonshot AI's Kimi, DeepSeek or Qwen - to hook US companies so they will become dependent on Chinese AI. US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said in July that the Trump administration could sanction Chinese AI companies if they were found to be guilty of intellectual property theft via distillation of American models. Distillation is the process of training smaller AI models using the output of larger ones as part of an effort to lower the costs of training a powerful new AI tool. Bessent's remarks echoed comments in April by Michael Kratsios, OSTP director, who accused China of stealing US artificial intelligence labs' intellectual property on an "industrial scale", spurring a State Department-led push to highlight such behavior to foreign counterparts.

Also read:

US to curb China's access to AI chips as Trump heads to Asia

China slams new US chip curbs, vows 'necessary measures'

CONGRESSIONAL INVESTIGATION But US officials have stopped short of restricting or taking punitive action against Chinese AI companies. The issue has attracted the attention of Congress. Republican US Representatives Andrew Garbarino of New York and John Moolenaar of Michigan, who chair the House Homeland Security Committee and the House select committee on China, respectively, launched an investigation into American companies' use of Chinese AI this year. They sent letters to Airbnb as well as Anysphere, the maker of the AI coding tool Cursor, whose Composer 2 AI model was built on a version of Kimi. A letter was also sent to DoorDash, whose co-founder said the company routes some tasks in an internal system through Kimi. Moonshot, DoorDash, and SpaceX, which bought Anysphere, did not immediately respond to requests for comment. Moolenaar welcomed news of the Trump administration's deliberations. "Disclosure is an important step in managing the potential risks posed by the diffusion of Chinese open-weight models in the United States,” he said in a statement to Reuters, noting that risks remain even if U companies run Chinese AI models on their own infrastructure. Canada-based Thomson Reuters, which owns Reuters, also uses Alibaba's Qwen, according to a TR spokesperson. She noted that the model was "substantially retrained" to align "with our standards for safety, accuracy and neutrality", and runs entirely within the company's own infrastructure. Chinese AI models were the three most popular by token usage in October on OpenRouter, an AI marketplace platform that tracks usage data. Tokens are units of data processed by AI models. Chinese AI models have even been used by the US government itself. Reuters reported in September that a US government website deployed an AI model from China's Alibaba to allow users to search proposed federal regulations even though the FBI accused the model's developer of copying Anthropic's technology. American open-weight models include Meta's Muse Glimmer, Nvidia's Nemotron and Reflection AI's Beam.

Source: Reuters/co

WASHINGTON: The Trump administration approved shipments of nearly 900,000 advanced AI chips made by Nvidia and AMD for Chinese companies from December 2025 through May 2026, the House Foreign Affairs Committee said on Thursday (Nov 19). The approvals for 879,000 chip shipments by the Commerce Department included 75,000 for Alibaba, 150,000 for Tencent, 43,000 for Baidu, and 4,000 for BYD, all on the Pentagon's list of alleged Chinese military-backed companies , the committee noted. The unusual release of chip export licensing data comes as the administration of President Donald Trump faces heightened scrutiny following news about former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s affair with an alleged Chinese spy , which has fueled renewed calls in Washington for a tougher stance on China. Companies had sought permission to ship over 3.4 million chips to China during the period, the documents showed. It was not immediately clear how many of the approvals resulted in actual China-bound shipments of chips, which included Nvidia's H200 and AMD's equivalent MI325X.

News surrounding Huang has turned a spotlight on instances of Nvidia AI chips being smuggled to China that went unpunished, dialing up pressure on the Trump administration to crack down on Chinese tech threats. "The fact that over 30 per cent of the AI chips sent to China were shipped to companies that the Department of War has designated as Chinese military companies is astonishing, and calls into question whether Commerce conducted any serious national security review before approving these licenses,” said Chris McGuire, a former US official and expert on the US-China technology battle. Nvidia said in a statement that the approvals were "subject to strict conditions and limited volumes." It added that "despite receiving some licenses, we have since stopped shipping H200s to China". AMD said it "complies with applicable US export control laws and regulations and maintains rigorous processes to ensure compliance across our global operations". Alibaba, Tencent, Baidu, BYD, the Commerce Department and the Chinese Embassy in Washington did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

Also read:

Nvidia faces deepening scrutiny over China chip ties, CEO affair

Why Alibaba, Baidu and BYD are on Pentagon’s list of 'Chinese military companies'

MOST DETAILED PUBLIC DISCLOSURE Former President Joe Biden had restricted Chinese access to the prized chips over fears that they would supercharge China's military and erode the US lead in artificial intelligence. But Trump in December gave the green light for Nvidia to ship its H200 chip to China, rolling back Biden-era restrictions and drawing fierce criticism from China hawks across the US political spectrum. Despite the approvals, questions swirled as to whether the AI chips were actually reaching Chinese shores. In May, Reuters reported the US had cleared about 10 companies to buy the H200, but that no deliveries had taken place. In testimony before the committee in July, Commerce Department official Jeffrey Kessler said shipments had begun but there had been 'very few'. Several major Chinese internet companies had each obtained about 10,000 H200 chips, Reuters has since reported, citing people familiar with the matter. "This is the most detailed public disclosure in the history of the Export Control Reform Act," committee Chair Brian Mast, a Republican from Florida, said upon releasing the data, referring to 2018 legislation that expanded Commerce's authority to restrict the export of sensitive technologies for national security reasons.

Source: Reuters/co

FAST

WINCHESTER: Four British men were convicted on Thursday (Nov 19) of raping or sex ually abusing a woman who was drugged by her then- husband in a case with echoes of that of Gisele Pelicot , the French woman who became a global symbol in the fight against sex ual violence. Joanne Young, like Pelicot , decided to waive her legal right to anonymity after discovering that her husband at the time had repeatedly drugged her and advertised her for sex online to strangers over more than a decade. Philip Young, a 50-year-old former local councillor, pleaded guilty in January to more than 50 charges against his ex-wife, including 11 counts of rape and charges relating to recording the abuse and publishing it online hundreds of times. "This abuse has cost me my life as I knew it," Joanne Young said outside court. "The person I trusted most in the world betrayed me in the most horrific way."

CALL TO RECONSIDER LAW ON CONSENT Police discovered the abuse only after an account linked to Philip Young posted bestiality images online in 2024 and then seized his devices, containing videos and images of the abuse. Young's crimes have striking similarities to those of Dominique Pelicot , who admitted drugging his then-wife Gisele and inviting dozens of men to rape her, prompting a 2024 trial that horrified the world and spurred France to revamp its rape law. Britain's National Crime Agency said this year it had uncovered a "truly international network" of drug-facilitated rape and sex ual assault, which it said was organised online and had members across the world. Law enforce men t officials from 10 countries, including the US, are now working on a global operation to target drug-facilitated sex ual assaults. Joanne Young said her case "raises serious questions about how the law deals with consent", adding: "I urge the govern men t to look at this as a priority so that wo men are properly protected in the future."

Women's rights campaigners outside Winchester Crown Court, where a jury is deliberating in the case of four men accused of raping or sexually assaulting Joanne Young, in Winchester, Britain, Nov 13, 2026. (Photo: REUTERS/Toby Shepheard)

FIFTH MAN HAD PLEADED GUILTY The men found guilty following a trial at Winchester Crown Court, in southern England, had responded to adverts posted by Philip Young, who admitted drugging his wife and inviting strangers to have sex with her, watching and filming while it happened. Richard Clive Wilkins, 62, was convicted of rape and assault by penetration, Norman Macksoni, 48, was also convicted of rape, Connor Sanderson-Doyle, 32, was found guilty of sex ual assault and assault by penetration, while Mohammed Hassan, 38, was convicted of one count of sex ual assault. In defences echoing those of many of the 50 co-defendants of Dominique Pelicot who were convicted in France, they said they thought Joanne Young consented and that it was a shared fantasy with her then- husband . She had sat in court as prosecutor Sarah Jones said her ex- husband had posted images online, showing his then-wife tied to her bed and blindfolded, as he "sought strangers to come and sleep with his wife – any age, any race". After the verdicts were announced, Judge Pushpinder Saini said she had shown "amazing bravery". A fifth man, Dean Hamilton, 47, had previously admitted rape, assault by penetration and sex ual assault. All five, along with Philip Young, will be sentenced next month and Saini said they faced a significant custodial sentence.

PELICOT NOT AN ISOLATED CASE The Pelicot trial horrified the world, but it now appears to be far from an isolated case . Specialist Crown Prosecution Service prosecutor James Foster said the case "marks the first time in England that a jury has convicted men of sex ually assaulting a woman , who had been drugged in abuse organised by her husband ". In April, law enforce men t bodies from 10 countries, coordinated by Europol, the EU's law enforce men t agency, set up "Project Medusa" to tackle the issue, led by investigators from Britain and Germany, and including the US, France and Canada. Those involved have since launched 113 investigations linked to that operation, leading to 57 arrests and 158 safeguarded victims, Europol said in June. The Crown Prosecution Service said British police had spoken with investigators who worked on the Pelicot case and that the toxicology expert whose evidence was used in France had also worked on the case involving Joanne Young. "I live with a pain that's hard to put into words ... it is terrifying that this could happen to anyone," Young said.

Source: Reuters/fs

MOGADISHU: Somalia ordered the United Arab Emirates ambassador on Thursday (Nov 19) to leave the country within 72 hours and withdrew its own envoy from Abu Dhabi, accusing the Emirates of unspecified violations of Somalia's sovereignty that amounted to an "open invasion". "Measures will be taken against anyone who cooperates with UAE in the invasion against Somalia," Information Minister Abdifatah Kasim Mohamud said in a broadcast on the state-run news agency. "All Somalis are urged to defend their country and unite against the open invasion of the UAE against the sovereignty, security, land and unity of Somalis." The minister did not elaborate on the actions the UAE had taken that had provoked Somalia's response.

In a speech on Tuesday, Somalia's President Hassan Sheikh Mohamud had accused the UAE of giving economic and political support to some regional Somali governments to oppose the federal government. There was no immediate response from the UAE foreign ministry. The UAE, which has helped fund and train Somalia's military in the past and has backed ports and other commercial ventures there, has long denied meddling in the country's affairs.

Related:

UAE investigators say flydubai co-pilot was planning 'terrorist act'

In January, Somalia said it had ended all agreements with the UAE, including port deals and defence and security cooperation, accusing the UAE of undermining its national sovereignty. Three self-governing Somali regions that have close relations with the United Arab Emirates dismissed that move at the time. The UAE has long leveraged its wealth to expand its influence across the Horn of Africa, using a mix of economic, military and diplomatic clout to assert regional power. For decades Somalia's federal government has had only limited authority across the country, and has failed to defeat Islamist militants, despite years of international support, including African peacekeepers and US air strikes. The UAE trained hundreds of Somali troops from 2014 to 2018, and still covers salaries and provides logistics for around 3,400 Somali military police and special forces troops in and around the capital, according to senior Somali sources. It has also forged bonds directly with regional governments, committing hundreds of millions of dollars to ports and military infrastructure on the coast along global shipping routes.

Source: Reuters/ht
